title: The Greek Gift Sacrifice
subtitle: Bxh7+: sacrificing the bishop to drag the king into the open
summary: White sacrifices the light-squared bishop on h7 to pull the black king out of safety, then follows up with Ng5+ and Qh5 to build a mating attack.

rootAnnotations.title: The three-attacker rule
rootAnnotations.body: The Greek Gift only works when White can throw three pieces at the black king: the bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, a knight that can jump to g5 with check, and a queen that can swing to h5 or the h-file. Here the diagonal is open, g5 is undefended (Black has no knight on f6), and Black's h-pawn hasn't moved — every condition is met.

rootAnnotations.title: Why Black is vulnerable
rootAnnotations.body: Black developed the queen's knight to d7 instead of the king's knight to f6, leaving g5 and h7 without a defender. That single move is the real cause of what follows — the sacrifice is just the punishment.

annotations.title: Giving up the bishop for the initiative
annotations.body: This isn't really a sacrifice in the losing-material sense — it's an investment. The bishop buys a tempo (forcing the king to move), rips open the black king's shelter, and hands the attack to the knight and queen that follow.

annotations.title: Declining is worse in practice
annotations.body: Black could try Kh8 instead, but then the bishop simply retreats (or even gets trapped and won later) while White is already up a clean pawn with a wrecked black kingside. Taking is the natural try and the one that tests the sacrifice.

annotations.title: The second attacker arrives — and clears a path
annotations.body: The knight both checks the king and vacates f3, opening the d1-h5 diagonal for the queen. This is the mechanical heart of the Greek Gift: bishop removes the pawn shield, knight harasses the king and clears the queen's road.

annotations.title: Running is more dangerous than it looks
annotations.body: Walking the king up the board feels brave, but it steps onto the very diagonal the bishop just vacated — the queen can reoccupy it with check.

annotations.title: The queen inherits the bishop's diagonal
annotations.body: Qd3+ checks along the same d3-h7 line the bishop used, and the king has no good answer: blocking with ...f5 permanently wrecks Black's kingside, while ...Kxg5 grabs the knight but leaves the king dangerously exposed to further checks. Either way, White's attack keeps rolling.

annotations.title: The third attacker completes the picture
annotations.body: Now White threatens Qh7#: the knight on g5 guards h7 and covers f7 and h8's escape square (h8 is x-rayed by the queen once it lands), so the black king has nowhere to run. This is the point of the whole combination — bishop, knight, and queen all converge on one square.

annotations.title: When the sacrifice is unsound
annotations.body: If Black's knight were still on f6 guarding g5 and h7, or if the h-pawn had already moved to h6, Bxh7+ would just lose a piece for nothing. Always check the three conditions before playing this sacrifice: open diagonal, undefended g5, and an unmoved h-pawn.
